name: Displaying the Days That are Above 32 Degrees Fahrenheit
description: Construct a program that reads a series of temperatures and reports the days that are above 32 degrees Fahrenheit. Assume that the temperature values are in Fahrenheit. Also assume that input values could have a decimal point.

comments.content: We need to first ask the user how many days of temperature data will be provided. To read the input value from user, we need to define a Scanner object. We can create a Scanner object using the operator new, as shown in this statement. The System.in object represents the standard input stream, which by default is the keyboard. It tells the java compiler that the input will be provided through keyboard.
We prompt the user to enter how many days of temperature data will be provided.
We need to read the number of days that the user enters and store it in a variable. We read the input integer by calling the nextInt() method because this input is an integer.
Note that if the user provides a non-integer number, an exception will be thrown because the input type is inconsistent with the expected data type, i.e., int.

We first need to define an array referred by variable temps for storing the temperatures that the user provides. This statement declares an array variable, temps, creates a double array with a length of numDays, and assigns its reference to temps. By default, each number in the array is 0.0. We will later update the array elements with the temperature values that we receive from the user. We need this array later to iterate over the temperature values and determine the days that are above 32 degrees Fahrenheit.

We want to read each temperature value and add each temperature value in the array to later determine the days that are above the average. To do this, we use a for loop to iterate over the array indexes and update them with temperature values. We need the array indexes to have a length of numDays and start at 0 with every integer number up to but not including numDays, where variable numDays is the number of days for which the user will provide the temperature values.

In the first part of the loop header, we define a control variable i and initialize it to 0. In the second part of the loop header, we test whether the control variable has reached the termination threshold. The loop is repeated if the control variable is less than numDays and terminates when the control variable reaches numDays. In the third part of the loop header, we increment the control variable by 1 after each iteration of the loop.

Note that the first part is executed once before the loop starts, the second part is executed before each iteration, and the third part is executed after each iteration of the loop. Also note that the increment operator (++) adds 1 to the value of variable i and the result is stored back into the variable i. Therefore, it is functionally equivalent to the statement i = i + 1.
We prompt the user to enter the temperature values.

We want to store the temperature value that the user has entered in the array temps. We read the value by calling nextDouble() method because temperature could have a decimal point. We assign this double to the element at index i of the array.
Note that this can only be done if user input could be translated into a valid double value.
We close the scanner as we do not want to process any input from the user in the rest of the program.

We first need to define an array to store true/false flags for each day to show whether a day is above 32 degrees Fahrenheit. This statement declares an array variable, aboveThreshold, creates a boolean array with a length of numDays, and assigns its reference to aboveThreshold. By default, each element in the boolean array is false. We will later set the array elements that correspond to days that are above 32 degrees Fahrenheit to true.

We need to iterate over the indexes in the array of temperatures using a for loop, determine which indexes store a temperature that is above 32 degrees Fahrenheit, and set the  value stored at those indexes in the array aboveThresholds to true. We need the array indexes to have a length of numDays and start at 0 with every integer number up to but not including the array length.

In the first part of the loop header, we define a control variable i and initialize it to 0. In the second part of the loop header, we test whether the control variable has reached the termination threshold. The loop is repeated if the control variable is less than the number of elements in the array and terminates when the control variable reaches the number of elements in the array. We can get the number of elements in the array by using the temps.length expression. In the third part of the loop header, we increment the control variable by 1 after each iteration of the loop.

Note that the first part is executed once before the loop starts, the second part is executed before each iteration, and the third part is executed after each iteration of the loop. Also note that the increment operator (++) adds 1 to the value of variable i and the result is stored back into the variable i. Therefore, it is functionally equivalent to the statement i = i + 1.

We need to compare the array element that we visited with the threshold of 32 degrees Fahrenheit. If that value is greater than 32 degrees, then we need to set its corresponding element in the array aboveThreshold to true.
If the value at index i of the array of temperatures is greater than 32, then the body of this if statement gets executed. Otherwise, the body of this if statement is skipped.

When the temperature value at index i is greater than 32 degrees, then we have to set its flag to true. We do this by setting the element at the index i of the array (referred by variable aboveThreshold) to true.
This statement prints the given text to the default standard output stream. This printed text is followed by the end-of-line character at the end.

We use a for loop to iterate over the array indexes in the array aboveThreshold and print the day number for the days that are above the threshold. We need the array indexes to start at 0 with every integer number up to but not including the array length.

Note that the first part is executed once before the loop starts, the second part is executed before each iteration, and the third part is executed after each iteration of the loop. Also note that the increment operator (++) adds 1 to the value of variable i and the result is stored back into the variable i. Therefore, it is functionally equivalent to the statement i = i + 1.
We check whether the element at index i of the array aboveThreshold is true. If so, we print the day number of that element.

Note that we could compare two boolean values using == operator. Also, note that we could use the following if statement to perform this check:
if (aboveThreshold[i]) {
If the value at index i of the array aboveThreshold is true, then the body of this if statement gets executed. Otherwise, the body of this if statement is skipped.
This statement prints the day number that has a temperature greater than 32 degrees Fahrenheit. It concatenates the given string and value of variable i+1 and prints the result of concatenation.
We use i+1 instead of i because day numbers start at 1 while the indexes of the array start at 0. So, we need to increment each index by 1 to get its corresponding day number.
The printed text is followed by the end-of-line character at the end.
